outline.rationale: The user is a total beginner aiming for product/feature decisions, so the outline starts from zero and orbits around decision-making rather than academic rigor. Node 1 sets realistic expectations (what research can/can't do) so they don't misuse it. Node 2 anchors everything to a decision, reinforcing the practical framing. Nodes 3–5 are the core doing-it skills: recruiting, interviewing (the highest-leverage method for a beginner), and lightweight prototype testing — the two most decision-driving methods. Node 6 addresses bias, which is the single biggest failure mode for beginners running interviews and gives disproportionate value. Node 7 closes the loop from raw findings to an actual build call, which is the user's explicit goal. I deliberately excluded statistical analysis, survey design, and large-scale quant per the confirmed understanding, and skipped any 'history/theory of UX research' filler. The nodes are MECE-ish: expectations, framing, recruiting, interviewing, testing, avoiding error, and synthesis have low content overlap.
